source.title_on_document: Prevalence and prevention of large language model use in crowd work

supplement.where: Appendices A-G, pp. 7-14 of this PDF.
supplement.holds: Data and synthetic-summary generation; participant and condition instructions; classifier training, calibration and prevalence methods; homogeneity and keyword-retention definitions; robustness checks and regression equations.

paper_design_summary: Study #1 observed LLM use among 168 Prolific workers summarizing medical abstracts, and Study #2 randomly assigned 720 Prolific workers to nine conditions combining requests and hurdles discouraging LLM use (pp. 2 and 5; pp. 8-9, Appendix B). Study #2 compared post-task classifier-defined synthetic and human summaries on ROUGE-L homogeneity and keyword retention (p. 4, Section 2.3; pp. 11-12, Appendix E). Its analysis of prevention effects on content outcomes was restricted to summaries labeled human by the classifier (p. 4, Section 2.3).

assignment.what_was_assigned: One common summarization task with no directions regarding LLM use; there were no assigned AI-assistance conditions. LLM use was measured from submitted summaries (p. 2, Section 1).
assignment.quote: In this study, we did not direct the participants regarding LLM use in any way,
assignment.locator: p. 2, Section 1, Study #1: Prevalence of LLM use (quote is the opening clause of the sentence).

arms.name: Uninstructed baseline
arms.description: All workers received the summarization task without directions about LLM use. AI status is null because the single cohort mixes detected LLM use and non-use; no tool was assigned (p. 2, Section 1).

participants.who: Prolific crowd workers who submitted medical-abstract summaries; the classifier was run on each submitted summary.
participants.quote: To estimate LLM usage on Prolific, a research-oriented crowd work platform, we asked n = 168 workers on 3 July 2023 to summarize scientific abstracts (following [7]; see Appendix).
participants.locator: p. 2, Section 1 (workers and all summaries analyzed); p. 5, Section 4.1, Data.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT/other LLMs; actual worker tools and model versions not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: LLM use was neither directed nor assigned. The researchers inferred use with a classifier and checked copy-pasting behavior; the classifier is a measurement tool, not the assistant given to workers (p. 2, Section 1).

task.description: Summarize one of 16 medical research abstracts, convey its most important information, and write at least 100 words (pp. 8-9, Appendix B, Experimental details and participant instructions).

assignment.what_was_assigned: A 3 x 3 factorial combination of requests discouraging LLM use (None, Indirect, Direct) and hurdles (None, Image, No Ctrl C+V). Randomization applied to prevention conditions. The main content comparisons instead group summaries after the task by detected LLM use (pp. 2, 4, 8-9 and 11).
assignment.quote: Using the same task and classifier as in Study #1, Study #2 was conducted on 23 July 2023, by randomly split n = 720 users into the nine conditions.
assignment.locator: p. 2, Section 2, Study #2: Prevention of LLM use; confirmed on p. 8, Appendix B, Experimental details.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT or other AI models used independently by workers; actual models and versions not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: The study varied requests not to use AI and barriers to copy-pasting. Use was assessed with a text classifier, follow-up self-reports, and heuristics. No particular generative model was assigned to a condition (pp. 2-3, Section 2; pp. 8-9, Appendix B).

task.description: Summarize one of 16 medical research abstracts, convey its most important information, and write at least 100 words (pp. 8-9, Appendix B, Experimental details and participant instructions).

outcomes.name: Across-worker summary homogeneity (ROUGE-L, averaged over source abstracts)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: ROUGE-L homogeneity based on the longest common subsequence between distinct workers' summaries of the same source abstract within a predicted class, followed by averaging over abstracts (pp. 11-12, Appendix E.1, Equation (2)). The main printed comparison uses classifier-defined synthetic and human groups (p. 4, Section 2.3). Appendix E.1 also describes grouping by heuristics and self-reports; no separate numerical homogeneity results for those variants are printed. The prevention/content analysis repeats the intervention model only among classifier-labeled human summaries (p. 4, Section 2.3; p. 13, Appendix G.1). Higher raw homogeneity means lower across-person diversity.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Classifier-labeled synthetic summaries (observed use, not an assigned arm)
contrasts.control_arm: Classifier-labeled human summaries (observed use, not an assigned arm)
contrasts.reported: Post-task classifier-defined groups: synthetic summaries had homogeneity 45.6% [43.2%, 48.2%], versus 27.1% [26.8%, 27.4%] for human summaries; the paper describes synthetic summaries as significantly more homogeneous. ROUGE-L compares summaries of the same abstract within each predicted class, then aggregates over abstracts. These are observed-use groups, not randomized prevention arms. Higher homogeneity means lower across-person diversity. The confidence level and interval-construction method are not specified in the content analysis.
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Section 2.3, Content-level analysis (reported values); pp. 11-12, Appendix E.1, Homogeneity (grouping and metric).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Request: Indirect and Direct; Hurdle: Image and No Ctrl C+V (separate intervention terms; classifier-labeled human summaries only)
contrasts.control_arm: Corresponding Request: None or Hurdle: None reference (classifier-labeled human summaries only)
contrasts.reported: In the analysis restricted to summaries labeled human by the classifier, the paper reports no significant effect of any prevention intervention on homogeneity. It repeats the intervention model using homogeneity as an outcome. No content-specific coefficient, interval, p value, or analyzed count is reported for these homogeneity comparisons. Selection by the post-task classifier label means these are not intention-to-treat AI-assistance effects.
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Section 2.3, final three sentences (content findings and restriction); p. 13, Appendix G.1 (intervention model and reference conditions).

diversity_detail.metric: ROUGE-L homogeneity using the longest common subsequence between distinct summaries; greater homogeneity means lower diversity (pp. 11-12, Appendix E.1, Equation (2)).
diversity_detail.embedding_model: None; the homogeneity metric uses lexical overlap. The classifier used to assign predicted classes is separate from the diversity metric (pp. 11-12, Appendix E.1).
diversity_detail.computed_over: Distinct pairs of summaries of the same source abstract within each predicted class, aggregated within abstract and then averaged across abstracts for that class. Main reported classes use classifier labels; Appendix E.1 also describes heuristics and self-reports (pp. 11-12).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Bracketed intervals accompany the main group scores, but their confidence level and construction, and the test establishing the homogeneity difference, are not specified. The restricted prevention/content analysis repeats the intervention model, but prints no homogeneity coefficient, interval, or p value (p. 4, Section 2.3; pp. 11-12, Appendix E.1; p. 13, Appendix G.1).
diversity_detail.notes: The main contrast compares post-task detected-use groups. Its direction is treatment_lower for diversity because the synthetic group has higher raw homogeneity. The prevention comparisons select the classifier-labeled human subset after assignment and are not intention-to-treat AI-assistance estimates.

outcomes.name: Keyword retention (proxy for summary quality)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Retention of key tokens from the source abstract concerning study participants, the intervention, and study outcomes, used as a proxy for summary quality (p. 12, Appendix E.2). The paper states that the metric favors extractive over abstractive summarization because changing the text risks changing key tokens. The main comparison uses classifier labels; similar synthetic-versus-human results are reported when groups are defined by self-reports or high-precision heuristics, without separate printed numerical estimates (p. 4, Section 2.3). The prevention/content analysis uses only classifier-labeled human summaries (p. 4, Section 2.3).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Classifier-labeled synthetic summaries (observed use, not an assigned arm)
contrasts.control_arm: Classifier-labeled human summaries (observed use, not an assigned arm)
contrasts.reported: Post-task classifier-defined groups: synthetic summaries preserved 40.1% [36.9%, 43.2%] of keywords, versus 31.2% [29.9%, 32.6%] for human summaries. The keywords represent essential information in the source abstract. The paper reports a similar effect using self-reports and high-precision heuristics to define groups. The confidence level and interval-construction method are not specified in the content analysis.
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Section 2.3, Content-level analysis (reported values); p. 12, Appendix E.2, Key token survival (measure).

contrasts.control_arm: Request: None (classifier-labeled human summaries only; hurdle indicators adjusted in the intervention model)
contrasts.reported: Among summaries labeled human by the classifier, directly requesting workers not to use LLMs decreased keyword retention by 6.2% (p = 0.009). This retains the printed percent wording; the paper does not report a content-specific coefficient with standard error, interval, or analyzed count. The analysis repeats the intervention model with keyword retention as an outcome and selects summaries by their post-task classifier label; it is not an intention-to-treat AI-assistance effect.
contrasts.locator: p. 4, Section 2.3, final three sentences (6.2%, p = 0.009, and restriction); p. 13, Appendix G.1 (intervention model).

contrasts.control_arm: Corresponding Request: None or Hurdle: None reference (classifier-labeled human summaries only)
contrasts.reported: In the analysis restricted to summaries labeled human by the classifier, the paper reports no significant effect on keyword retention for the prevention interventions other than the direct request. No content-specific coefficients, intervals, p values, or analyzed counts are reported for these remaining comparisons. These selected-subset results are not intention-to-treat AI-assistance effects.

eligibility.reason: Study #2 randomly assigned requests and copy-pasting hurdles intended to discourage LLM use, not generative-AI assistance (p. 2, Section 2; pp. 8-9, Appendix B). The main content comparisons group summaries after submission by detected LLM use, so they are observational; the prevention/content analysis further restricts the sample to summaries labeled human by the classifier (p. 4, Section 2.3; pp. 11-12, Appendix E.1). Criterion 1 is not met and core is no under creativity-codebook.md, Sections 3-4. Study #2 reports 720 randomized people, but no separate analyzed count for the scored content outcomes or the selected human-labeled subset (pp. 2 and 5, Sections 2 and 4.1; p. 4, Section 2.3). Because form-spec.md defines criterion 2 using people analyzed, that criterion is unclear for the study with relevant outcomes. Homogeneity is computed on workers' outputs and satisfies criterion 3 (p. 4, Section 2.3; pp. 11-12, Appendix E.1). Study #1 analyzed summaries from 168 workers, but reports only LLM-use prevalence and detection checks, with no creativity or across-person diversity outcome (p. 2, Section 1). Retain observational context; the online_rct design label describes the prevention experiment, not a randomized AI-assistance content contrast.

one_line_finding: In Study #2 (720 workers), classifier-labeled synthetic summaries were more homogeneous than human-labeled summaries (45.6% [43.2%, 48.2%] versus 27.1% [26.8%, 27.4%]); this main comparison uses detected AI use rather than randomized prevention condition (p. 2, Section 2; p. 4, Section 2.3).
notes: Data URL is printed on p. 8, Appendix A, Data availability. The model-training code URL is printed on p. 10, Appendix C. The PDF also supplies experiment materials/code at https://github.com/epfl-dlab/LLM-crowdwork/experiments/ (p. 8, Appendix B). These are the links exactly as printed; their current online contents were not inspected.
